flags: minor: R041-01 and R041-09 both turn on the individual-vs-group distinction from the last paragraph, so solving one helps with the other
R041-01.notes: C covers the flawed news story, the lab finding that individuals help less, and the group-level result. A adds an unsupported city/small-town comparison. B contradicts P5 ('do not necessarily contradict'). D overstates agreement and leaves out the passage's twist. C is about as long as A, so length gives no cue.

R041-02.notes: P1 describes the Genovese report and says it 'inspired a generation of research.' B is not argued anywhere. C belongs to P2 and D to P4, so both are content from the wrong paragraph.

flags: minor: very easy, because the key closely restates the passage ('less personally responsible, assuming that someone else will act')
R041-03.notes: The passage states this directly. A, B and C are not mentioned.

R041-04.notes: The second explanation is that people take cues from others: if no one seems alarmed, the situation does not seem like an emergency. D is a strong trap because it applies the first explanation (diffusion of responsibility) instead. A is the opposite of the effect. C misreads 'responsible.' The stem's words 'second explanation' make the answer unambiguous.

R041-05.notes: 'Staged emergencies' means arranged or set up. C is the trap based on the literal theater sense. B and D do not fit the context.

R041-06.notes: P3's main point comes after 'But': the story was less accurate than first reported. C covers only its first sentence. B is P4's content. A contradicts P3 ('reproduced in many laboratory studies').

flags: minor: R041-07 and R041-08 overlap. Both hinge on the fact that Philpot's study used real recorded footage rather than staged emergencies, so knowing either answer gives away the other. Consider replacing one.
R041-07.notes: Directly stated in P4: 'examined security-camera footage of more than two hundred public conflicts.' This item is very easy.

flags: minor: overlaps with R041-07 (see note there)
R041-08.notes: Real conflicts recorded in public versus emergencies staged in the lab. A describes Darley and Latané's study. C contradicts the ~90% intervention rate. D is unsupported.

R041-09.notes: P5 says each individual in a crowd is less likely to act, yet a group is more likely to produce a helper. Only D has both halves. B is the strongest trap (classic bystander effect at both levels). A reverses the individual-level claim. C shows no effect at all. A good application item.

flags: minor: A is the longest choice, though D is close in length
R041-10.notes: The author accepts the individual-level finding ('a person in a crowd may indeed be less likely to act') but recasts its lesson as being about divided responsibility rather than indifference. B is too strong: the author separates the flawed story from the lab finding. C: the author is clearly critical. D: 'hostile' is too extreme.

passage_fact_check: Accurate overall. Genovese was killed in March 1964, and the NYT story ran March 27, about two weeks later. The '38 witnesses' figure was later debunked, including by the NYT's own 2004 reporting and its 2016 editor's note: few witnesses saw much, at least one person called police, and neighbor Sophia Farrar went to her. Darley and Latané ran the seizure study (1968) and the smoke-filled-room study (Latané & Darley, 1968). Philpot et al. (2019, American Psychologist) analyzed 219 conflicts in Lancaster, Amsterdam and Cape Town, found about 91% intervention, and found intervention more likely with more bystanders. Minor imprecision: 'outside her apartment building' (the fatal second attack happened in a vestibule or hallway of the building), which is acceptable at ACT level.
